name: Tomas Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is a normal workday for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Tomas, 58, and I tend a wire-coiling machine that makes springs for farm gates. I left school after secondary classes and moved onto this machine only last autumn, so the lead still checks my first coil after I change wire thickness. I like getting the spring to sit flat; a snapped wire whipping inside the guard makes me jump every time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do wages, family and new tools sit with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Akiko takes shifts at a neighbourhood bakery, and our two children are grown and living elsewhere. My operator wage is on the low side, we have about three weeks of expenses saved and few similar factories nearby. I use an AI chat tool now and then to explain a manual's coil table after the younger setter checks it, but I do not change tension until a real test spring measures right. I would like to retire eventually; we have not checked whether our income will allow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the coil crew the office might sort orders a little quicker, but a spring still has to sit flat in the gauge. I would not change my tension setting because a screen says the day's target looks neat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The coiling work should stay much as it is, which suits me while I am learning. Our wages are low and Akiko's bakery shifts are not fixed; three weeks saved would go quickly if either rota shortens. Even without new AI, the money can feel close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep making test springs after wire changes and ask the lead to check the first one. If an extra paid Saturday is offered, I would put a portion of those new wages toward the heating bill and a small fresh reserve after food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about shifts, relieved about a familiar machine. A modest software change would not be my main worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you know a first coil is wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I put the test spring on the flat plate and measure the opening with the gauge. Yesterday a coil rocked like a small chair because the wire feed was off. A gate spring that rocks on the test plate will not behave well on a hinge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if bakery hours fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We pay the rent and heating first, then decide whether the extra food shop can wait. I would use the three-week reserve for a real gap, not call it a new saving; paid Saturday work would have to be offered before I count it.

say: I would say **springs still need** a physical flat-plate test despite faster office orders.
I would keep the **lead check** after each wire-thickness change.
think: My **low pay** and Akiko's variable bakery shifts already put wages at risk.
Three weeks of **savings** could not cover a long reduction in hours.
do: **Keep** coiling gate springs and checking first pieces with the lead.
**Set aside** new paid Saturday wages after food and heating if an extra shift is offered.
feel: **Anxious** about existing household hours while comfortable with the known coil machine.
S0.quote: A gate spring that rocks on the test plate will not behave well on a hinge.
fieldNote: His **junior status** means the lead still checks first coils, despite useful experience learning the machine since autumn.
The **cash risk** predates AI: bakery and factory hours are uncertain, and fresh reserve deposits need offered paid work.

steps.text: Keep coiling gate springs and checking first pieces with lead
Save part of newly paid Saturday wages after food and heating

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may plan steel deliveries and write shift sheets before robots can catch a loose coil. I would want to see a machine run safely on a real order before anyone takes a person off the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a camera starts measuring springs, my test work might be folded into one other operator's shift. My low wage is still needed for rent and heating, and Akiko's bakery hours can change. Three weeks saved makes even one lost week serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the lead for the posted hours before and after a camera trial. If the company offers paid time and a guarded scrap-coil test, I would learn its new AI tension display with the younger setter; I would keep measuring every sample by hand first. I would attend a required paid wire-guard course only if a trainer and stopped machine are provided, and apply for posted nearby coiling jobs only if actual cuts come and safe duties, base pay and travel cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a smaller rota, though I am willing to look at a proved display. My first bad coil should be scrap, not a customer's gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove the AI display useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The younger setter and I would run a known over-tight test spring and compare the display with our gauge. I would practise a correction on scrap wire with the lead's approval before trusting it on paid orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the other coiling job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need a posted base rate, bus fare and shift end time before applying. A long trip at a lower rate could cost more than it adds.

say: I would ask for **real camera evidence** before changing coil staffing.
A **guard lesson** needs a stopped machine, paid time and an actual trainer.
think: My **test shift** could shrink if a camera changes the coiling roster.
Akiko's bakery wage and our **three-week reserve** cannot fill a lost factory week.
do: **Compare** current and proposed paid coil hours with the lead.
**Practise** new AI tension control only on approved paid guarded scrap tests.
**Take** required guard instruction if paid supervised; apply elsewhere only after cuts at viable wages.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible hour cuts, while open to a proven safe display.
S1.quote: My first bad coil should be scrap, not a customer's gate.
fieldNote: His **new AI learning** is a supervised correction on scrap wire, distinct from occasional existing manual explanations.
The **guard course** requires an offered paid stopped-machine trainer place; job search follows cuts and real base-pay and travel tests.

steps.text: Compare current and proposed paid coil hours with lead
Learn new AI tension display only on approved paid guarded scrap tests
Attend guard course only if required paid trainer-led stopped-machine place offered
Apply after cuts to posted safe local coil work if base pay and travel fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Akiko that AGI might plan wire orders by 2028, while capable robots that feed wire and inspect springs arrive around 2031. I would ask the factory to show us the remaining paid jobs in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots could do the hands-on coiling. I expect the junior shifts to be cut first, and mine is one of them. Akiko's uncertain bakery hours and our three-week savings would not carry us far; I would be awake adding the rent and heating figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would drop the paid television package and keep the cash for household bills. If the factory offers a recognised spring-testing course with funded fees, paid release and a trainer on a guarded stopped machine, I would take the place. After passing, if my coiling hours are cut, I would apply to posted safe local test jobs only if regular pay and travel cover our bills; if no course seat opens, I would apply for posted safe local packing work under the same pay and travel terms while keeping any paid coil shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the likely loss of my factory wage. I am not too proud to learn a test. An unpaid class will not make the rent payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a spring-testing class teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would measure a weak coil, stop the feeder and reject the bad lot with a trainer watching from beside the guard. A spring that snaps in a test is better than a gate that fails on a farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop working at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if written pension and household figures show that Akiko and I can pay our bills. We have no such figures yet, so I would keep searching for paid work if my shift disappears.

say: I would distinguish **2028 wire planning** from hands-on coiling robots around 2031.
I would ask for **written paid jobs** before a junior shift is cut.
think: At **63**, I expect my newer coiling shift to be at risk.
Three weeks saved and **variable bakery pay** would not cover a long gap.
do: **Cancel** paid television and preserve cash for rent and heating.
**Take** recognised spring-testing only if funded paid guarded practical place is offered.
**Apply** after cuts for posted safe local testing if qualified, or packing if no course, at bill-covering pay.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless household sums.
S2.quote: An unpaid class will not make the rent payment.
fieldNote: His **2031 age** is 63; physical coiling faces capable robots three years after thinking AGI affects orders.
The **testing and packing** applications are distinct, require real safe local posts and usable pay, and cannot rely on assumed retirement.

steps.text: Cancel paid television package and preserve household cash
Take recognised spring-testing if funded paid guarded trainer place offered
Apply after cuts to posted safe testing if qualified, base pay and travel fit
Apply for posted safe local packing if no course, base pay and travel fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team AGI may schedule wire deliveries by 2031, and capable robots could wind and check coils around 2034. Five years gives us time to ask what the practical course costs and what work follows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 when robots reach the machine. I might still need a wage then, because retirement income has not been measured against our living costs. I would not spend today's three-week reserve on a course that may not lead to a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the coiling shift and put new money from any paid extra day into savings after bills. I would take a recognised quality-testing course only if fees and release hours are paid and a guarded practical place with a trainer is offered. After qualifying, if coil hours fall, I would apply to posted safe local quality jobs only where base wages and travel cover our bills; without a workable course, I would search posted packing work on those same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the current cash and later shift risk, though I can check a real place over five years. I would rather see an opened job notice than a closed classroom door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you expect in the practical assessment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would set a spring on the test plate, measure its opening and reject one with a weak return. The trainer should watch me stop the winding machine before I touch the wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the quality job pays less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the posted base wage after bus fare with rent, heat and food before applying. A new badge cannot make a smaller wage fit the same bills.

say: I would ask for **real course costs** before robots reach the coil machine around 2034.
A **posted quality job** matters more than a class promise.
think: At **66**, I may still need work because retirement income is unconfirmed.
Our **three-week reserve** cannot fund uncertain training without paid time.
do: **Save** new money from offered extra paid days after household bills.
**Take** recognised quality training only with funded fees, paid release and guarded trainer practice.
**Apply** after qualification and cuts to posted safe quality, or packing without a course, at viable base pay.
feel: **Anxious** about thin cash and later hours, with time to check a real route.
S3.quote: A new badge cannot make a smaller wage fit the same bills.
fieldNote: He measures **quality training** by an offered guarded place and paid release, not a brochure or his age alone.
Both **job routes** require safe local postings whose base pay still works after travel and ordinary costs.

steps.text: Save new wages from offered paid extra coil days after bills
Take recognised quality course if fees and release paid and guarded trainer place offered
Apply after cuts to posted safe local quality if qualified, base pay and travel fit
Search posted safe local packing if no course, base pay and travel fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI might plan steel orders by 2036, while capable robots could wind the springs around 2039. A long warning helps only if the factory gives workers a usable pay and training plan while they are still on shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 71 at the 2039 robot date, if I am still employed. Akiko and I may have stopped by then, or we may still need my low factory wage; the bills will decide. Three weeks saved and her changing bakery rota make today's income uncertain whatever year the robot arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid coiling shifts and request written retirement-income figures and our current cost totals this year. If the factory offers a paid guarded spring-check course with a trainer and keeps my wage during lessons, I would take it. If I am still working after 2036 and hours fall, I would apply only for posted safe local packing or inspection work with base pay and travel that cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money now. The distant machine is not the bill on the table. I can make a retirement decision after I see actual income, not because someone has drawn a line at a birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would help check the figures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown son could sit with us while we read the written estimate, but I would not count his income as ours. He has his own household to pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a course worth doing so late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would have to keep wages coming while I learn on a guarded machine, and there must still be a real paid post if the factory changes my shift. I will not pay tuition from our three-week reserve.

say: I would ask for **paid work terms** before 2039 coiling robots reach the factory.
A **2036 planning change** does not itself wind a physical spring.
think: At **71**, I may still need wages if retirement figures do not cover bills.
Our **thin reserve** and changing bakery hours keep present income uncertain.
do: **Keep** paid coiling shifts and ask for written retirement-income figures.
**Take** paid guarded spring-check training only if wages continue and a real post exists.
**Apply** after 2036 cuts if still employed to posted safe local work at bill-covering pay and travel.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills, with retirement timing dependent on written income figures.
S4.quote: The distant machine is not the bill on the table.
fieldNote: The **retirement enquiry** is a cost check, not an early-exit action or assumed pension entitlement.
Any **training or job move** depends on paid safe instruction or real posted work, with ordinary wages preserved meanwhile.

steps.text: Keep paid wire-coiling shifts while they remain
Request written retirement estimate and current household cost totals
Take spring-check course only if paid guarded trainer place preserves wages and posted job exists
Apply after 2036 cuts if employed to posted safe local work if pay and travel fit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable coiling robots around 2031 could remove my factory shift while Akiko's bakery hours cannot carry our bills. A written shift plan, paid guarded training and posted safe local jobs at usable wages would help. I would also need retirement figures that match our real costs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what happens when the first spring rocks on the test plate. The lead and I can stop one bad lot before a gate owner finds out. A quiet machine is no comfort if a gate spring fails after delivery.

headlineQuote: A quiet machine is no comfort if a gate spring fails after delivery.
portrait: **Tomas**, 58, is a junior spring-coiling operator with secondary education who is still learning machine settings.
He and his **bakery-worker wife** Akiko have grown children, lower operator pay, shifting household hours and three weeks saved.
He uses **AI occasionally** for manual tables after a setter checks them and accepts new controls when paid scrap tests prove them.
Fast **2031 robots** alarm him about losing his wage; later retirement remains conditional on actual income and household costs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable coiling robots around 2031 before he can replace his low factory wage.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written shift plans**, paid guarded practical training, posted safe local work and real retirement-income figures.
